_comment: PLACEHOLDER risk levels and monitoring plans, written for the demo from general public knowledge of spaceflight effects. Not NASA rules, not medical advice. Keys under body_risks match content.json body_parts; keys under monitoring match health_rules.json indicators.

station.headline: Weightless, close to Earth: gravity loss is the main threat, help is only a call away.

skeleton.why: No gravity means bones carry no weight and slowly lose density.

muscles.why: Leg and back muscles shrink fast when they never hold you up.

heart.why: Blood shifts toward the head and the heart works less, so it can weaken.

eyes.why: Fluid pushing toward the head can press on the back of the eyes.

brain.why: Small crew, busy schedule and odd light cycles disturb sleep and mood.

immune.why: Some radiation and stress, but Earth's magnetic field still shields the station.

stomach.why: Regular resupply keeps food and water varied.

monitoring.why: The main defence against bone and muscle loss in 0 g.
Catches changes caused by fluid moving toward the head.
Shows if the heart is adapting or struggling.
16 sunrises a day confuse the body clock.
Early sign of stress from confinement.
Thirst feels weaker in 0 g, so crews drink too little.

lunar_base.headline: Some gravity, more radiation, and dust everywhere: protect your cells and keep moving.

immune.why: No magnetic field on the Moon, so radiation reaches the crew more easily.

skeleton.why: 1/6 of Earth's gravity still lets bones weaken over months.

muscles.why: Walking is easier on the Moon, so muscles do less work.

brain.why: Two-week nights and a cramped base disturb sleep and mood.

heart.why: Partial gravity keeps blood flow closer to normal.

eyes.why: Less fluid shift than in 0 g; lunar dust is the bigger eye irritant.

stomach.why: Supplies arrive in days, not months.

monitoring.why: A fever can be the first sign of a weakened immune system.
Long lunar days and nights break the normal sleep rhythm.
Low gravity still costs bone and muscle.
Isolation in a small base builds up over weeks.
Radiation and fatigue can slow thinking before you notice.
Baseline check after moonwalks and hard work.

mars_transit.headline: Months in 0 g, high radiation, and a 20-minute delay to Earth: the crew is its own doctor.

skeleton.why: Months without gravity: the longest stretch of bone loss of any mission.

muscles.why: Muscles must be strong enough to walk on Mars on arrival day.

immune.why: Deep-space radiation with no planet or magnetic field for shielding.

brain.why: Isolation, no window to Earth, and fixed crew for months: mood and sleep suffer.

eyes.why: Long 0 g exposure raises the chance of vision changes.

heart.why: Fluid shift and less work for the heart over many months.

stomach.why: No resupply: food is packed months ahead and loses nutrients.

monitoring.why: Arrive on Mars able to stand and walk.
Earth can't step in quickly, so problems must be caught early.
Poor sleep is the first domino for mood, focus and immunity.
Checks the brain for radiation and fatigue effects.
Long-term 0 g changes how the heart and vessels work.
Early warning for infection when the nearest hospital is months away.
Packaged food and low activity can shift metabolism.

mars_base.headline: Back on a surface at 0.38 g after a long trip: rebuild strength, watch radiation, still far from help.

muscles.why: Weakened muscles from transit now have to carry suits and tools.

skeleton.why: Mars gravity helps a bit, but bones lost during transit recover slowly.

immune.why: Thin atmosphere and no magnetic field let radiation through.

brain.why: Still isolated, but a planet underfoot and a 24h40m day help routine.

heart.why: Readjusting to gravity can cause dizziness when standing.

eyes.why: Gravity pulls fluid back down, easing pressure behind the eyes.

stomach.why: Long-stored food; any fresh food must be grown on site.

monitoring.why: Spots dizziness and strain while the body readjusts to gravity.
Standing up can drop pressure after months in 0 g.
Rebuild the strength lost in transit.
Infection watch with a 20-minute delay to Earth's doctors.
A Mars day is 40 minutes longer, which slowly shifts the body clock.
Isolation continues for the whole surface stay.

rover.headline: Hard physical work in a cramped cabin, away from the base's medical kit.

muscles.why: Long drives plus heavy work outside in a suit.

heart.why: Exertion in a suit raises heart rate and body heat.

stomach.why: Limited water and food on board, so dehydration comes fast.

brain.why: Tight space, long shifts and little privacy wear down focus.

immune.why: Less shielding in a rover than inside the base.

skeleton.why: Same gravity as the base; heavy work actually loads the bones.

eyes.why: No extra eye risk beyond the base itself.

monitoring.why: Suit work makes you sweat; the rover carries limited water.
Catches overexertion before it becomes dangerous.
Overheating inside the suit is a real risk.
A tired driver far from base is a safety risk.
Short, cramped sleep adds up fast on long trips.
